structures.name: epiglottis
structures.definition: Leaf-shaped flap of elastic cartilage behind the root of the tongue.
structures.function: Tips back over the entrance to the larynx during swallowing.
structures.why: It helps steer food and drink into the oesophagus instead of the airway.

notes.nursing: After a stroke, an impaired swallow lets food slip past it: screen swallowing before giving anything by mouth.
notes.medicine: Epiglottitis causes drooling, stridor and a “tripod” posture; don’t examine the throat, secure the airway.

structures.name: thyroid cartilage
structures.definition: The largest cartilage of the larynx, shaped like an open book facing forward.
structures.function: Shields the vocal cords and anchors them at the front.
structures.why: Its two plates meet at an angle that forms the laryngeal prominence.

notes.medicine: Its prominence (Adam’s apple) is larger after puberty in males because the vocal cords lengthen.
notes.nursing: A landmark for finding the cricothyroid membrane just below it in an airway emergency.

structures.name: cricoid cartilage
structures.definition: Signet-ring-shaped cartilage at the bottom of the larynx, the only complete ring in the airway.
structures.function: Supports the larynx and holds the airway open where it joins the trachea.
structures.why: A complete ring keeps the airway from collapsing at its narrowest fixed point.

notes.medicine: Marks the C6 level; the cricothyroid membrane above it is the site of an emergency surgical airway.

structures.name: arytenoid cartilages
structures.definition: Pair of small pyramid-shaped cartilages sitting on the back of the ring-shaped cartilage below.
structures.function: Pivot and slide to open and close the vocal cords, which attach to them.
structures.why: Moving these small cartilages lets tiny muscles control voice pitch and protect the airway.

notes.medicine: Can be dislocated by intubation, causing hoarseness afterwards.

structures.name: septal cartilage
structures.definition: Plate of cartilage forming the front part of the wall between the two nasal cavities.
structures.function: Divides the nose into two airways and supports the tip of the nose.
structures.why: Cartilage, unlike bone, lets the nose bend under impact.

notes.sports: A blow to the nose can cause a septal haematoma, which must be drained to protect the cartilage.

structures.name: trachea
structures.definition: Tube about 10–12 cm long, held open by C-shaped rings, running from the larynx into the chest.
structures.function: Conducts air to and from the lungs and sweeps mucus upward with its cilia.
structures.why: C-shaped rings keep it open but let the oesophagus behind it expand when swallowing.

notes.nursing: Tracheostomy care keeps the tube clear; humidify inspired air because the nose is bypassed.
notes.medicine: Divides at the carina at about T4–T5, level with the sternal angle.

structures.name: right main bronchus
structures.definition: Short, wide airway branching from the trachea to the right lung.
structures.function: Carries air into the right lung, where it divides into three lobar bronchi.
structures.why: It runs more vertically than its partner because the heart sits to the left.

notes.nursing: Inhaled objects and aspirated fluid usually go into the right lung; an endotracheal tube pushed too far enters it.
notes.medicine: Wider, shorter and more vertical than the left: the classic site of aspirated foreign bodies.

structures.name: left main bronchus
structures.definition: Longer, narrower airway branching from the trachea to the left lung, under the aortic arch.
structures.function: Carries air into the left lung, where it divides into two lobar bronchi.
structures.why: It passes under the aortic arch and in front of the oesophagus to reach the smaller left lung.

notes.medicine: Its course under the arch explains why the aorta and left bronchus are close on chest imaging.

structures.name: bronchial tree
structures.definition: Branching airways that divide about 23 times from the main bronchi down to the smallest bronchioles.
structures.function: Distributes air to every part of the lungs.
structures.why: Repeated branching spreads air across an exchange surface the size of a tennis court.

notes.nursing: Chest physiotherapy positions drain particular segments of it.
notes.physio: Postural drainage uses the anatomy of its segments to clear secretions.

structures.name: right middle lobe
structures.definition: The lobe found only in the right lung, between the upper and lower lobes, shown here by its airways.
structures.function: Ventilates the front of the lower right chest, beside the heart.
structures.why: The right lung has three lobes because the heart takes up space on the left.

notes.medicine: Its collapse or pneumonia blurs the right heart border on a chest X-ray.

structures.name: lingula
structures.definition: Tongue-shaped part of the left upper lobe beside the heart, shown here by its airways.
structures.function: Ventilates the part of the left lung next to the heart.
structures.why: It is the left lung’s equivalent of the right middle lobe.

notes.medicine: Consolidation here blurs the left heart border on a chest X-ray.

structures.name: right lung
structures.definition: Larger of the two lungs, with three lobes, in the right side of the chest (shown here by its ten segmental airway trees).
structures.function: Takes in oxygen and gives off carbon dioxide across its alveoli.
structures.why: It is larger than its partner because the heart leans to the left.

notes.nursing: Listen at the front, sides and back; the lower lobe is heard mainly from behind.
notes.physio: Deep breathing and early mobilisation after surgery prevent its bases from collapsing.

structures.name: left lung
structures.definition: Smaller of the two lungs, with two lobes and a notch for the heart (shown here by its segmental airway trees).
structures.function: Takes in oxygen and gives off carbon dioxide across its alveoli.
structures.why: Its cardiac notch makes room for the heart.

notes.nursing: Compare both sides when listening; reduced breath sounds on one side can mean collapse, fluid or pneumothorax.

structures.name: diaphragm
structures.definition: Dome-shaped sheet of muscle separating the chest from the abdomen.
structures.function: Contracts and flattens to draw air into the lungs; does most of the work of quiet breathing.
structures.why: Enlarging the chest from below is the most efficient way to inflate the lungs.

notes.nursing: Sitting a breathless patient upright lets it move more freely.
notes.medicine: Supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3–C5); irritation refers pain to the shoulder tip.

structures.name: external intercostals
structures.definition: Muscles filling the spaces between the ribs, their fibres running down and forward.
structures.function: Lift the ribs to widen the chest when breathing in.
structures.why: They stiffen the chest wall so it doesn’t get sucked inward on each breath.

notes.physio: Thoracic expansion exercises work them to improve breathing after chest surgery.
